clue.text: Yell, like great soprano!

parts.note: to yell is to call out

explanation.surface: Someone bellows in admiration, comparing a cry to the power of a famous diva.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma splits the clue into two ordinary words placed side by side before the definition. Maria Callas was the celebrated Greek-American opera singer.
explanation.definitionFit: Maria Callas was among the most famous operatic sopranos of the twentieth century, so she is a fair example of a great one.

clue.text: Loco partner of Bill smuggles in illicit whisky

indicators.note: to smuggle something in is to carry it hidden inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: lovers 'bill and coo', so coo is the partner of bill
hooch is slang for illegally made or smuggled liquor

explanation.surface: A crazy accomplice of someone called Bill sneaks bootleg whisky across the border.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loco' reads as Spanish for crazy, but here it is short for locomotive. 'Bill' is not a man's name: the phrase 'bill and coo' describes lovers' billing and cooing.
explanation.definitionFit: A choo-choo is the nursery word for a railway engine, and loco is the everyday short form of locomotive.

clue.text: A little secret always turns up in due course

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up makes the letters read from bottom to top, so their order flips
only a little of the following words is used, so a short run of letters is taken from inside them

parts.note: the last three letters of 'secret' and the first two of 'always'

explanation.surface: A small secret has a way of coming out eventually.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the gap between two words and then are read backwards up the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that happens in due course happens afterwards, at a future time, which is the adverb's everyday meaning.

clue.text: Tablet poisoning animal, one runs home

parts.note: the asp is a venomous snake
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs
to be in is to be at home

explanation.surface: A pill has poisoned some creature, and one of them dashes back home.
explanation.walkthrough: Four short pieces join in order. R for runs comes from cricket scorecards.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspirin is a common painkiller usually sold as small pressed pills, so it is an example of a tablet.

clue.text: Popular musician in Australia having saturated market

indicators.note: to saturate is to soak right through, so one piece has entered and sits inside another

parts.note: Oz is the familiar name for Australia

explanation.surface: A pop star in Australia has flooded the record market with releases.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Popular musician' suggests a chart act, but the definition simply means a well-loved composer. Oz is a common nickname for Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: Mozart remains one of the best-loved and most widely performed classical composers, so he is a popular musician in a broad sense.

clue.text: Too upset about a nightmare play

indicators.note: 'about' means surrounding, so one piece wraps around another
something upset is knocked over and disordered, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is overly disturbed by a play that feels like a bad dream.
explanation.walkthrough: The three letters of the first word are shuffled and then wrapped round the word for an awful experience.
explanation.definitionFit: Othello is Shakespeare's tragedy of the Moor of Venice, so it is an example of a stage drama.

clue.text: Arranged ASAP, April review

indicators.note: arranged means put into a new order, so the letters are set out afresh

explanation.surface: An office memo: the staff assessment has been scheduled urgently for April.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a manager booking an annual review; 'Arranged' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An appraisal is a formal assessment of performance, which is what a work review is.

clue.text: Line in lease looked up for one of those residing in toolshed?

definitions.text: one of those residing in toolshed?

indicators.note: 'in' places one piece inside another
in a down clue, looking up means reading from the bottom to the top, so the order flips

parts.note: to let a property is to lease it

explanation.surface: A tenancy agreement is checked for a clause about things kept in the garden shed.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the word for leasing is turned upwards; the line sits inside it. The question mark flags a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A trowel is a small hand tool for gardening, typically kept in a shed, so it is an example of what lives there.

clue.text: Boxer with cut covering up, tho' woozy

indicators.note: to cover is to go over and around, so one piece encloses another
woozy means dizzy and muddled, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A fighter with a gash gets patched up, though still groggy from the blows.
explanation.walkthrough: The boxing surface hides that the cut is a verb for using a toothed blade.
explanation.definitionFit: A southpaw is a left-handed boxer who leads with the right, so the word names a type of fighter.

clue.text: Twins eating out, sampling drink

indicators.note: out can mean disordered or wrong, so the letters are put into a different order

explanation.surface: A pair of twins dine at a restaurant and try a little wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eating out' looks like a phrase for dining, but 'out' alone is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Wine-tasting is the activity of trying small amounts of different wines to judge them, so it means sampling an alcoholic beverage.

clue.text: Fashionable dance music

parts.note: a hop is an informal dance

explanation.surface: Trendy dance tunes are being described.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as one phrase, but only the last word defines; the first two make the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Hip-hop is a genre of popular rhythmic music with rapping, originating in New York in the 1970s.

clue.text: Sign of old injury, frightening cut

indicators.note: cutting a word shortens it, so its final letter is lopped off

explanation.surface: A healed mark recalls a terrifying wound from long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut' sits beside 'injury' as if it were the wound, but it instructs removing the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A scar is the mark of healed tissue left on the skin after a wound has closed up.

clue.text: Chief criminal element in campanologist?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the head of a gang
second meaning, read literally: the one who leads a ring of bell-ringers

explanation.walkthrough: A campanologist is a bell-ringer, and bell-ringers perform as a ring; read literally, the leader of that ring is the second meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The head of a criminal gang is its ringleader, and the second meaning splits the compound into its literal parts.

clue.text: Search is around country for underwear

parts.note: to comb an area is to search it thoroughly

indicators.note: 'around' means surrounding, so one piece wraps another

explanation.surface: Someone hunts across a whole country for a particular kind of undergarment.
explanation.walkthrough: The short word wraps the country, and the search word goes in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Combinations are an old-fashioned one-piece undergarment covering body and legs, so they are a kind of underclothing.

clue.text: Change one's tune in second song

parts.note: to second someone is to back them
a track is a song on a record

explanation.surface: A singer switches melody partway through their next number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'second' looks like an ordinal number, but here it is the verb meaning to support.
explanation.definitionFit: To change one's tune is an idiom for reversing a stated position, which is exactly what it means to retreat from an earlier claim.

clue.text: Party animal, teacher is into the dancing

indicators.note: going into something puts one piece inside another
dancing letters move about, so they land in a new order

parts.note: a don is a university teacher

explanation.surface: A teacher who loves to party is getting into the dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: A don is an Oxford or Cambridge lecturer. 'the dancing' is the jumbled word, and the teacher plus 'is' sit inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A hedonist lives for pleasure, and a party animal is the informal term for someone devoted to fun and revelry.

clue.text: Unfriendly attitude in Arctic bear

parts.note: to bear a burden is to shoulder it

explanation.surface: A polar bear is treating someone in a distinctly frosty way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arctic bear' suggests a polar bear; here 'bear' is the verb for carrying a load.
explanation.definitionFit: Giving someone the cold shoulder is an idiom for deliberately ignoring or snubbing them, a hostile manner.

clue.text: Stand in line on centre ground

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for line

indicators.note: something ground has been crushed up and broken down, so its letters are remade

explanation.surface: A footballer queues up, or holds a position, on the middle of the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'centre ground' looks like a political or sporting phrase; 'ground' is the anagram signal. In a down clue, 'on' puts the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A lectern is a sloping desk on a pedestal for holding a book or notes, so it is a kind of reading stand.

clue.text: See irregular verbs in middle of poem

indicators.note: 'in' places one piece inside another
the middle of a word is its central letters, so only those are kept
irregular means out of the usual order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A grammar note: look at the irregular verbs in the middle of the poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'irregular verbs' is a familiar grammar phrase, but 'irregular' is the anagram signal for the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: To observe is to notice or watch, a direct synonym of the verb meaning to perceive with the eyes.

clue.text: Cue is raised and brown finally pocketed by girl

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising letters makes them read upwards, so their order flips
something pocketed is tucked inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: gal is an informal word for a girl

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the last letter is kept

explanation.surface: A snooker scene: the cue is lifted and the brown ball goes into a girl's pocket.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is snooker, with a cue, a brown ball and a pocket, but 'Cue' is the definition, meaning a prompt.
explanation.definitionFit: A cue is a prompt to act, such as an actor's line to enter, and a signal is exactly such a prompt.

clue.text: I chop, as it's chopped nuts!

indicators.note: chopped means cut into pieces, so the letters are broken up and reassembled

explanation.surface: A cook announces they are chopping because the recipe calls for chopped nuts.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated 'chop' makes the surface read like kitchen instructions, while 'nuts' could also mean crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Pistachios are the green edible seeds of a Middle Eastern tree, eaten and cooked as a kind of nut.

clue.text: Cold wine unfinished — a little sweet?

indicators.note: something unfinished lacks its end, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap
hock is a German white wine from the Rhine

explanation.surface: Someone leaves a chilled wine half-drunk and wonders whether it is slightly sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a little sweet' looks like describing the wine; it is the definition, a small confection. Hock is a traditional British name for Rhine wine.
explanation.definitionFit: A choc is the informal short form of chocolate, a small piece of confectionery, and the shortened word mirrors 'a little'.

clue.text: First of chords, large number — for a song!

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: a heap is a large number of things

explanation.surface: A musician strikes a chord and a big crowd turns out to hear a song.
explanation.walkthrough: With chords in the surface, 'for a song' sounds musical; it is the idiom for a low price.
explanation.definitionFit: Buying something for a song is an idiom for paying very little, so it means inexpensive.

clue.text: Con elected ally

parts.note: a candidate who is elected is in
a mate is a friend or ally

explanation.surface: A trickster has been voted in alongside a partner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Con' reads as a swindle or a Conservative; here it is short for convict.
explanation.definitionFit: A con is slang for a convict, and an inmate is someone held in prison, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Plant in Grenada I built

indicators.note: to build is to construct, so the letters are put together into something new

explanation.surface: A boast: I constructed a factory on the Caribbean island of Grenada.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' tempts as a factory, given 'built'; it is the botanical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The gardenia is an evergreen shrub prized for its fragrant white flowers, so it is an example of a flowering plant.

clue.text: Man on left I love

indicators.note: in an across answer, putting one thing on another means it follows after, so the order of pieces is fixed

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for left
a king is a man in chess

explanation.surface: A man stands on my left, and I am fond of him.
explanation.walkthrough: In chess the pieces are called men, so a king is a man. 'on' places it after the other two pieces in an across answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A liking is a fondness or affection for someone, so it is a milder synonym of the noun meaning devotion.

clue.text: Steward originally found in bus garage, tyrant

indicators.note: to be found in something is to sit inside it

parts.note: a depot is where buses are kept

indicators.note: originally points to the beginning, so only the first letter is kept

explanation.surface: A bossy official discovered at the bus depot is a petty dictator.
explanation.walkthrough: One letter drops into the middle of the word for a vehicle yard.
explanation.definitionFit: A despot is a ruler who holds absolute power and uses it cruelly, the same as an oppressive autocrat.
